question: How should an ML team record experiment and tuning history (MLflow tracking), organise code with version control, and choose between serial, parallel and concurrent execution to finish an MVP at reasonable cost?

results.claim: Tracking tuning runs in MLflow gives a historical record that serves both experimentation and long-term monitoring, including detecting when performance has degraded enough to rebuild.
results.setup: Author's argument from the airport-forecasting running example (thousands of airports, one model each); no measurement.

results.claim: With SparkTrials, wrap the whole tuning run in one MLflow context so each hyperparameter evaluation is logged as a child of a parent run; with the pandas_udf approach there is no parent-child grouping, so custom naming and tagging are needed for searchability.
results.setup: Chapter 7 Hyperopt implementations (SparkTrials on the driver vs pandas_udf, listing 7.10) on the forecasting project.

results.claim: SparkTrials is the better choice for a single-model project; pandas_udf is far better for thousands of models.
results.setup: Forecasting project with thousands of per-airport models; no timings given.
results.quote: the pandas_udf approach is far superior.

results.claim: Print statements in production ML code are never read again and give no history; logging a run's tags, metrics, params and artifacts to MLflow replaces RDBMS tables, NoSQL stores or ELT over system logs.
results.setup: Author's experience and Fig 8.4 comparison of notebook prints, log daemon, and MLflow tracking.

results.claim: Keeping all information about a tuning and training event in one place external to the executing system saves time when re-creating training conditions and answering business questions, and lowers the chance of project abandonment.

results.claim: One branch per story cut from master, with unit tests plus a full-run integration test before a peer-reviewed merge, avoids merge problems and broken code; version control practice is identical to traditional software engineering.
results.setup: Fig 8.6 workflow: feature branches, pull requests, sprint release branch managed by lead DS, tests, merge to master.

results.claim: Scalability here means cost: VM time is the bill, so maximising hardware utilisation per unit time keeps cost down; per-model training parallelism cut cost more than parallelising hyperparameter evaluation.

results.claim: Prefer a single machine when the problem fits; add infrastructure complexity (concurrency, parallelism, both) only when data, algorithm or task scale forces it.

The chapter text has no pyfunc custom model, model registry, stage transitions, model signature, or serving content, and no complete code listings: only the two API calls mlflow.set_tag and mlflow.log_artifact are named. Listing 7.10 and the SparkTrials code are in chapter 7 and the companion notebook, not here.
Concurrency vs parallelism definition is loose: the text defines concurrency as 'executing many tasks at the same time', which blurs it with parallelism.
Built on Hyperopt, Spark, and the MLflow tracking API of about 2021-22; MLflow Registry and newer features are not covered.
The code layout and Spark companion notebook are external to this PDF and were not read.
practices: Wrap a SparkTrials tuning run in a single MLflow run context so child iterations group under a parent run (8.1.1).
For per-model Hyperopt in pandas_udf, create a named run per iteration with custom names and tags so the GUI and REST API can search them (8.1.1).
Replace print statements in production ML code with MLflow logging of tags, metrics, parameters and artifacts (8.1.2).
Use mlflow.set_tag(<key>, <value>) for extra run info and mlflow.log_artifact(<local path>) for plots, data and models (8.1.2).
Log per-entity metrics and parameters plus forecast charts so historical runs are searchable (8.1.2).
Cut one branch per sprint story from master, add unit tests, pass an integration test, and merge by peer-reviewed pull request (8.1.3).
Keep a repository layout separating common, data, model, scoring, tuning, visualizations, docs and src entry point (Fig 8.5).
Retrain models at least daily, weekly or monthly rather than letting them go stale (chapter intro, author's opinion).
Use the simplest execution paradigm that fits; move to concurrent or distributed only when needed (8.2.1).
Isolate independent tasks (per-airport data, tuning) to parallelise; check library docs for whether an algorithm distributes (8.2.2).

terms.definition: A black swan event is an unforeseeable and many times catastrophic event that changes the nature of acquired data.
Concurrency, by definition, is the act of executing many tasks at the same time.
Parallelism, on the other hand, works by dividing tasks into subtasks that can be executed in parallel, simultaneously, on discrete threads and cores of a CPU or GPU.
When we talk about scalability here, we’re actually referring to cost.
